learn.hook: Every entry in the books of a company like Amul begins with a piece of paper or a digital slip: a bill, a receipt, a cheque. No paper, no entry.
points: A business transaction is an exchange of economic value (money or money's worth) between the business and another party. Every transaction has a two-fold effect.
A source document is the written evidence of a transaction, prepared at the time it happens. It is the basis for recording.
Common source documents: cash memo (cash sale), invoice or bill (credit sale), receipt (cash received), pay-in-slip (cash or cheque deposited in bank), cheque (order to a bank to pay), salary slip.

Debit note: sent by the buyer to the seller when goods are returned, informing that the seller's account has been debited. Credit note: sent by the seller to the buyer for goods returned, informing that the buyer's account has been credited.

example.q: Riya returns damaged goods worth ₹4,000 to her supplier Mehta Traders. Which document does she send, and which does Mehta Traders send her?
steps: Riya, the buyer, returns goods and debits the supplier's account: she sends a debit note.
Mehta Traders, the seller, accepts the return and credits Riya's account: it sends a credit note.
example.answer: Riya sends a debit note; Mehta Traders sends a credit note.

learn.reallife: When you deposit cash at a bank branch, you fill a pay-in-slip; its counterfoil, stamped by the cashier, is the source document for your entry.

items: Every business transaction has a two-fold effect.
This is the dual aspect: one account gives, another receives.
A credit note is prepared by the buyer when returning goods.
The buyer prepares a debit note; the seller issues a credit note.
A cheque is an order to a bank to pay a stated sum.
It is a written unconditional order to the bank.
A cash memo is prepared for credit sales.
A cash memo is for cash sales; an invoice is for credit sales.
Source documents provide evidence for recording transactions.
Entries are supported by source documents.

quiz.q: Which source document is issued by a seller for a credit sale?
quiz.explain: An invoice shows quantity, price and terms of a credit sale.
steps: A credit sale needs a document showing quantity, price and terms.
That document is the invoice (bill), issued by the seller.
A cash memo is for cash sales; a receipt is for cash received.
Answer: Invoice (bill)
quiz.mistake: Confuses a cash memo with an invoice

quiz.q: When a buyer returns goods to a supplier, the buyer sends a
quiz.explain: The buyer debits the supplier's account and informs him through a debit note.
steps: The buyer returns goods and debits the supplier's account.
The buyer informs the supplier through a debit note.
A credit note is sent the other way, by the seller.
Answer: Debit note
quiz.mistake: Swaps debit note and credit note

quiz.q: Which document is used to deposit cash into a bank account?
quiz.explain: A pay-in-slip is filled when depositing cash or cheques into a bank.
steps: Depositing cash or cheques into a bank needs a pay-in-slip.
A cheque is an order to a bank to pay, not a deposit form.
So the answer is pay-in-slip.
Answer: Pay-in-slip
quiz.mistake: Thinks a cheque is used to deposit cash

quiz.q: A credit note is sent by the
options: Buyer to the seller, when goods are returned
Bank to the customer, for interest
Seller to the buyer, when goods are returned
quiz.explain: The seller credits the buyer's account for returned goods and informs him through a credit note.
steps: For goods returned, the seller credits the buyer's account.
The seller informs the buyer through a credit note.
So a credit note goes from seller to buyer.
Answer: Seller to the buyer, when goods are returned
quiz.mistake: Thinks credit notes are always sent by buyers

quiz.q: Which statement best defines a business transaction?
options: An exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party
A plan to buy goods next year
Hiring an employee before work starts
quiz.explain: Only an actual exchange of economic value is a transaction.
steps: A transaction is an exchange of economic value between the business and another party.
Conversations, plans or hiring before work starts involve no exchange.
So the correct definition is an exchange of money or money's worth.
Answer: An exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party
quiz.mistake: Treats plans or talks as transactions

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Source documents are the basis for recording entries in the books.
Reason (R): They provide written evidence that a transaction took place.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Entries must be supported by evidence; source documents provide that evidence.
steps: A: source documents are the basis of recording. True.
R: they are written evidence that a transaction happened. True.
Entries must rest on evidence, which source documents give, so R explains A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks entries can be made without proof

quiz.q: A salary slip given to an employee is a source document for recording
quiz.explain: It shows the salary payable and paid to an employee.
steps: A salary slip shows the salary payable and paid to an employee.
So it supports the entry for salary paid.
Answer: Salary paid
quiz.mistake: Links salary slips with sales

quiz.q: Case: A retailer sells goods for cash and gives the customer a slip showing items and amount. This slip is a
quiz.explain: A cash memo is the proof of a cash sale.
steps: The retailer sells for cash and gives a slip with items and amount.
Proof of a cash sale is a cash memo.
An invoice would be used for a credit sale.
Answer: Cash memo
quiz.mistake: Confuses sales documents with return documents

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I returned a faulty fan to the shop. Who writes a debit note and who writes a credit note?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The buyer sends a debit note, the seller sends a credit note when goods are returned!
teach.nudge: Close! Which one does the buyer send? And what does the seller send back?

revise.summary: A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth with a two-fold effect. Source documents such as cash memos, invoices, receipts, pay-in-slips, cheques and debit/credit notes are the evidence for recording it.
focus: Match each source document to its transaction
Who sends a debit note and who sends a credit note
What makes an event a business transaction
remember: Cash memo → cash sale; invoice → credit sale; pay-in-slip → bank deposit
Debit note: buyer → seller for goods returned
Credit note: seller → buyer for goods returned
traps: Don't mix up debit note and credit note: the buyer sends the debit note
A cash memo is not used for credit sales

learn.hook: In a large firm, no accountant writes an entry from memory. A voucher, signed and numbered, travels with every transaction like a boarding pass.
points: An accounting voucher is prepared from source documents. It records the accounts to be debited and credited, and is authorised by a responsible person.
Contents: name of firm, voucher number, date, accounts debited and credited with amounts, narration (brief explanation), and signatures of the preparer and the authoriser.

Cash vouchers: debit voucher (for cash payment) and credit voucher (for cash receipt). Non-cash or transfer (journal) vouchers are used for transactions without cash, e.g. credit purchases or depreciation.
Transaction voucher: one debit and one credit. Compound voucher: one debit with several credits, or one credit with several debits. Complex voucher: several debits and several credits.

example.q: Rent ₹15,000 is paid in cash. Which voucher is prepared, and what does it show?
steps: Cash goes out, so a cash payment voucher, i.e. a debit voucher, is prepared.
Account debited: Rent A/c ₹15,000; account credited: Cash A/c ₹15,000.
Narration: 'Being rent paid for the month'; signed by the preparer and authorised by the manager.
example.answer: A debit voucher: Dr Rent ₹15,000 / Cr Cash ₹15,000.

learn.reallife: Government offices in India pass every payment through a numbered voucher signed by the drawing and disbursing officer, so auditors from the CAG can trace each rupee.

games.title: Which voucher?
items: Goods bought on credit from Gupta
Goods sold on credit to Sharma

quiz.q: A voucher prepared for cash received from a customer is a
quiz.explain: Cash receipts are recorded on credit (receipt) vouchers.
steps: Cash is received from a customer.
Cash receipts are recorded on a credit (receipt) voucher.
A debit voucher is for cash payments.
Answer: Credit voucher
quiz.mistake: Thinks cash received is a debit voucher because cash is debited

quiz.q: Goods purchased on credit from Rahul for ₹25,000 are recorded on a
quiz.explain: No cash is involved, so a non-cash transfer voucher is used.
steps: Goods bought on credit from Rahul: no cash moves.
Non-cash transactions use a transfer (journal) voucher.
So the answer is transfer voucher.
Answer: Transfer (journal) voucher
quiz.mistake: Thinks every purchase needs a cash voucher

quiz.q: A voucher records one debit and two credits. It is a
quiz.explain: One debit with multiple credits (or vice versa) makes a compound voucher.
steps: One debit with two credits = more than one account on one side.
One debit and several credits (or the reverse) is a compound voucher.
A complex voucher needs several debits AND several credits.
Answer: Compound voucher
quiz.mistake: Calls any voucher with more than two accounts complex

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT normally a content of an accounting voucher?
quiz.explain: Vouchers contain identification, accounts, amounts, narration and signatures, not unrelated personal data.
steps: A voucher has voucher number, date, accounts debited/credited, amounts, narration and signatures.
Personal phone contacts of a customer are not part of it.
So that is the item NOT included.
Answer: The customer's personal phone contacts
quiz.mistake: Thinks vouchers are general record sheets

quiz.q: Salary of ₹30,000 and rent of ₹10,000 are paid together by one cheque of ₹40,000. The voucher is a
quiz.explain: Two debits (salary, rent) and one credit (bank) make it a compound voucher.
steps: Debits: Salary ₹30,000 and Rent ₹10,000 (two debits).
Credit: Bank ₹40,000 (one credit).
Several debits with one credit = compound voucher.
Answer: Compound voucher
quiz.mistake: Counts the cheque as several credits

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting vouchers are prepared on the basis of source documents.
Reason (R): Source documents contain the evidence of transactions that vouchers record.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Vouchers translate the evidence in source documents into debits and credits.
steps: A: vouchers are prepared from source documents. True.
R: source documents hold the evidence that vouchers record. True.
Vouchers turn that evidence into debits and credits, so R explains A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks vouchers come before the source document

quiz.q: Case: A firm buys machinery ₹2,00,000 and furniture ₹50,000, paying ₹1,50,000 by cheque and owing the rest to the supplier. Which voucher is prepared?
quiz.explain: Two debits (machinery, furniture) and two credits (bank, supplier) make a complex voucher.
steps: Debits: Machinery ₹2,00,000 and Furniture ₹50,000.
Several debits and several credits = complex voucher.
Answer: Complex voucher
quiz.mistake: Ignores one side of the transaction

quiz.q: Under a transaction voucher, how many accounts are debited?
quiz.explain: A transaction voucher has exactly one debit and one credit.
steps: A transaction voucher has exactly one debit and one credit.
So one account is debited.
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Mixes up transaction and compound vouchers

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why write a voucher? Why not jump straight to the journal?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Vouchers turn source documents into signed, authorised debits and credits. Now the journal can trust them!
teach.nudge: Good! Who signs a voucher, and what does it say is debited and credited?

revise.summary: Accounting vouchers are prepared from source documents and show the accounts debited and credited, with narration and authorisation. They are cash (debit/credit) or transfer vouchers, and transaction, compound or complex in form.
focus: Choose debit, credit or transfer voucher for a transaction
Classify a voucher as transaction, compound or complex
Contents of a voucher
remember: Debit voucher = cash payment; credit voucher = cash receipt; transfer voucher = no cash
Transaction: 1 Dr + 1 Cr; compound: 1 on one side, many on the other
Complex: several debits and several credits
traps: Don't call a cash receipt voucher a debit voucher; it is a credit voucher
One debit with two credits is compound, not complex

topics.title: The accounting equation: A = L + C

learn.hook: No matter what happens in a business, this equation never breaks: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Every transaction is like a see-saw that stays level.
points: Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Variants: Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital.
Every transaction changes at least two items so that the equation still balances.

Possible effects: both sides increase (goods bought on credit); both sides decrease (creditor paid); one asset up and another down (furniture bought for cash); one liability up and another down (creditor paid by a bill payable).
A tabular analysis lists each transaction with its effect on each asset, liability and capital; totals of both sides match after every line.

example.q: Start: cash ₹1,00,000 = capital ₹1,00,000. (1) Goods bought on credit ₹30,000. (2) Furniture bought for cash ₹20,000. Show the equation after both.
steps: (1) Stock +30,000 (asset), creditors +30,000 (liability).
(2) Furniture +20,000, cash −20,000: assets change between themselves.
Assets: cash 80,000 + stock 30,000 + furniture 20,000 = ₹1,30,000.

learn.reallife: Even a startup in Bengaluru raising ₹10 crore from investors records it as cash up and capital up by the same ₹10 crore, keeping the equation balanced.

games.title: Effect on the equation

items.q: A ₹3,00,000 then goods ₹40,000 bought on credit. New A?
A ₹5,00,000 then creditor ₹60,000 paid. New A?

quiz.q: Assets of a firm are ₹10,00,000 and capital is ₹6,50,000. What are the liabilities?
quiz.explain: Liabilities = Assets − Capital.
quiz.mistake: Adds capital to assets

quiz.q: Furniture is purchased for cash ₹25,000. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: One asset increases and another asset decreases; totals unchanged
quiz.explain: Furniture goes up and cash goes down by the same amount.
steps: Furniture (asset) rises by ₹25,000.
Cash (asset) falls by ₹25,000.
One asset up and another down by the same amount; totals unchanged.
Answer: One asset increases and another asset decreases; totals unchanged
quiz.mistake: Treats buying an asset as an increase in total assets

quiz.q: Which transaction increases both assets and liabilities?
options: Goods sold for cash at cost
quiz.explain: Stock (asset) and creditors (liability) both rise.
steps: Goods on credit: stock (asset) rises.
Creditors (liability) rise by the same amount.
So goods purchased on credit increases both assets and liabilities.
Answer: Goods purchased on credit
quiz.mistake: Picks a transaction that only changes assets

quiz.q: A creditor of ₹18,000 is paid in cash. What happens?
options: Assets and liabilities both decrease by ₹18,000
quiz.explain: Cash (asset) falls and creditors (liability) fall by the same amount.
steps: Paying a creditor ₹18,000 in cash.
Cash (asset) falls by ₹18,000; creditors (liability) fall by ₹18,000.
So assets and liabilities both decrease by ₹18,000.
Answer: Assets and liabilities both decrease by ₹18,000
quiz.mistake: Records only one side of the payment

quiz.q: Opening: assets ₹4,00,000, liabilities ₹1,00,000. The firm takes a bank loan of ₹50,000 in cash. What is the capital after this?
quiz.explain: A loan raises assets and liabilities equally; capital is unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a loan increases capital

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every transaction keeps the accounting equation in balance.
Reason (R): Every transaction has two equal effects.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because each transaction has equal dual effects, both sides change by the same amount or stay unchanged.
steps: A: every transaction keeps the equation balanced. True.
R: every transaction has two equal effects. True.
Equal dual effects are why both sides stay equal, so R explains A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the equation balances only at year-end

quiz.q: A creditor of ₹20,000 accepts a bill payable for the amount. What is the effect?
options: One liability decreases and another liability increases
quiz.explain: Creditors fall and bills payable rise; totals are unchanged.
steps: Creditor accepts a bill payable: creditors fall by ₹20,000.
Bills payable rise by ₹20,000.
One liability down, another up; totals unchanged.
Answer: One liability decreases and another liability increases
quiz.mistake: Thinks accepting a bill pays the creditor in cash

quiz.q: Case: Raghav starts with ₹2,00,000 cash, buys goods for cash ₹80,000 and buys a computer on credit ₹40,000. What are total assets?
quiz.explain: Cash 1,20,000 + stock 80,000 + computer 40,000.
steps: Stock = ₹80,000; computer = ₹40,000
quiz.mistake: Adds the cash purchase as a new asset without reducing cash

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I buy a laptop for my business with cash, does the business get richer?'
teach.praise: Tweet! One asset up, another down, and Assets = Liabilities + Capital still balances. Not richer, just rearranged!
teach.nudge: Close! When the laptop comes in, what goes out? Does the equation total change?

revise.summary: The accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital always balances because every transaction has two equal effects on its items.
focus: Find the missing item (assets, liabilities or capital)
Show the effect of a transaction on both sides
Build a tabular analysis of a series of transactions
remember: Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital
Effects: both sides up, both down, asset-asset swap, liability-liability swap
traps: Buying an asset for cash does not change the totals
A bank loan raises assets and liabilities, not capital

topics.title: Accounting equation: revenue, expenses, drawings and full numericals

learn.hook: Sell goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹14,000 and something magical happens in the equation: capital grows by exactly ₹4,000.
points: Revenue and profit increase capital; expenses, losses and drawings reduce capital.
Sale of goods at a profit: cash or debtors rise by the sale price, stock falls by the cost, and capital rises by the profit.
Expenses paid in cash (rent, salary): cash falls and capital falls. Outstanding expenses: liabilities rise and capital falls.
Drawings in cash or goods: assets fall and capital falls.
After a series of transactions, the final balances of the equation give the balance sheet.

example.q: Capital ₹1,00,000 in cash. (1) Bought goods ₹40,000 cash. (2) Sold goods costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 on credit. (3) Paid rent ₹5,000. (4) Withdrew ₹3,000 cash. Find the final capital.
steps: (3) Rent is an expense: capital −5,000.
(4) Drawings: capital −3,000.
Check: cash 52,000 + stock 10,000 + debtors 45,000 = ₹1,07,000 = capital (no liabilities).

learn.reallife: A food-truck owner at Juhu beach sees capital rise with every profitable evening and fall every time she takes cash home: the equation tracks her real stake.

games.title: Sale at a profit: trace the effects

quiz.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 are sold for ₹65,000 in cash. By how much does capital increase?
quiz.explain: Only the profit (sale price − cost) adds to capital.
steps: Answer: ₹15,000
quiz.mistake: Adds the whole sale price to capital

quiz.q: Salary of ₹12,000 is outstanding at year-end. Its effect on the equation is
options: Liabilities increase and capital decreases by ₹12,000
No effect, since cash is not paid
quiz.explain: An outstanding expense creates a liability and reduces capital through the expense.
steps: Outstanding salary: an expense not yet paid.
It creates a liability (outstanding salary) of ₹12,000.
The expense reduces capital by ₹12,000; cash is not affected.
Answer: Liabilities increase and capital decreases by ₹12,000
quiz.mistake: Ignores expenses not paid in cash

quiz.q: The owner takes goods costing ₹6,000 for personal use. The effect is
options: Stock decreases and capital decreases by ₹6,000
quiz.explain: Drawings reduce both the asset given away and the owner's capital.
steps: Goods taken for personal use = drawings.
Stock (asset) falls by ₹6,000.
Drawings reduce capital by ₹6,000.
Answer: Stock decreases and capital decreases by ₹6,000
quiz.mistake: Treats drawings as a sale

quiz.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000. During the year: profit ₹70,000, drawings ₹25,000, additional capital ₹40,000. What is the closing capital?
quiz.explain: Closing capital = Opening + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings.
quiz.mistake: Adds drawings instead of deducting

quiz.q: Rahul starts business with cash ₹2,50,000. He buys goods on credit ₹60,000 and pays rent ₹8,000 in cash. What is the total of assets?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reduce cash for the rent

quiz.q: Meena starts business with cash ₹2,50,000, buys goods on credit ₹60,000 and pays rent ₹8,000 in cash. What is her capital now?
quiz.explain: Capital falls by the rent expense; the credit purchase does not change capital.
quiz.mistake: Thinks credit purchases reduce capital

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Payment of rent reduces capital.
Reason (R): Expenses reduce the owner's equity.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Expenses reduce profit, and so reduce the owner's claim (capital).
steps: A: payment of rent reduces capital. True.
R: expenses reduce owner's equity. True.
Rent is an expense, so it reduces capital exactly because of R.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks only drawings reduce capital

quiz.q: Interest of ₹4,000 is received in cash. Its effect on the equation is
options: Assets increase and capital increases by ₹4,000
quiz.explain: Income raises cash and, through profit, capital.
steps: Interest received is income.
Cash (asset) rises by ₹4,000.
Income increases capital by ₹4,000.
Answer: Assets increase and capital increases by ₹4,000
quiz.mistake: Treats income received as a liability

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'When a shop sells something, why doesn't the whole sale price get added to the owner's capital?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Only the profit adds to capital, because the stock that went out cost something too!
teach.nudge: Hmm, the shop gave away stock as well. Which part of the sale actually adds to capital?

revise.summary: Revenues and profits increase capital; expenses, losses and drawings reduce it. A sale at profit changes stock by cost and cash or debtors by sale price, with the profit added to capital.
focus: Effect of sale at profit, expenses, outstanding expenses and drawings
Find closing capital after profit, drawings and additional capital
Find total assets after a series of transactions
remember: Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings
Sale at profit: capital rises by (Sale price − Cost)
Outstanding expense: liabilities up, capital down
traps: An outstanding expense still affects the equation even though no cash is paid
Don't add the whole sale price to capital; only the profit

topics.title: Debit, credit and the rules for each type of account

learn.hook: Debit is not 'bad' and credit is not 'good'. In accounting, they simply mean left and right, like the two sides of a cricket pitch.
points: An account is a summarised record of all transactions about one item (Cash A/c, Rent A/c). A T-account has the debit side on the left and the credit side on the right.
Assets and expenses/losses: increase is debited, decrease is credited.
Liabilities, capital and revenues/gains: increase is credited, decrease is debited.
Drawings reduce capital, so drawings are debited.
To find the entry: identify the two accounts, decide each one's type, decide increase or decrease, and apply the rule.

example.q: Paid salary ₹20,000 by cheque. Which account is debited and which credited?
steps: Accounts affected: Salary A/c and Bank A/c.
Salary is an expense and it increases: debit Salary.
Bank is an asset and it decreases: credit Bank.

learn.reallife: When Indian Railways buys a new locomotive on credit, its accountants debit the Locomotive (asset increases) and credit the supplier (liability increases).

items.text: An increase in an asset is ___.
An increase in a liability is ___.
An increase in an expense is ___.
The debit side of an account is on the ___.

quiz.q: Goods purchased on credit from Anil ₹30,000. Which entry is correct?
quiz.explain: Purchases (expense-type) increase, debit; Anil, a creditor (liability), increases, credit.
steps: Accounts: Purchases and Anil.
Purchases increase: debit Purchases ₹30,000.
Anil, a creditor (liability), increases: credit Anil ₹30,000.
No cash is paid, so Cash is not involved.
Answer: Dr Purchases ₹30,000 / Cr Anil ₹30,000
quiz.mistake: Credits cash though nothing was paid

quiz.q: An increase in a liability is recorded on the
quiz.explain: Liabilities increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side.
steps: Rule: liabilities increase on the credit side.
They decrease on the debit side.
So an increase in a liability goes on the credit side.
Answer: Credit side
quiz.mistake: Applies the asset rule to liabilities

quiz.q: Commission received in cash ₹5,000. The accounts debited and credited are
quiz.explain: Cash (asset) increases, debit; commission (revenue) increases, credit.
steps: Cash (asset) increases: debit Cash.
Commission received (revenue) increases: credit Commission received.
Entry: Dr Cash / Cr Commission received.
Answer: Dr Cash / Cr Commission received
quiz.mistake: Debits the income account

quiz.q: Which account normally has a credit balance?
quiz.explain: Capital, liabilities and incomes normally show credit balances.
steps: Capital, liabilities and incomes normally have credit balances.
Machinery (asset), rent (expense) and drawings have debit balances.
So Capital account has a credit balance.
Answer: Capital account
quiz.mistake: Thinks drawings has a credit balance because it relates to capital

quiz.q: Loan of ₹1,00,000 repaid by cheque. Which entry is correct?
quiz.explain: The liability (loan) decreases, debit; the asset (bank) decreases, credit.
steps: Loan (liability) decreases: debit Loan.
Bank (asset) decreases: credit Bank.
Entry: Dr Loan / Cr Bank.
Answer: Dr Loan / Cr Bank
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry for taking a loan

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Drawings are debited.
Reason (R): Drawings reduce the capital of the owner, and a decrease in capital is debited.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Capital decreases are debited, and drawings reduce capital.
steps: A: drawings are debited. True.
R: drawings reduce capital, and a decrease in capital is debited. True.
R gives the rule behind A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks drawings are credited because cash goes out

quiz.q: Machinery sold for cash at its book value ₹40,000. Which entry is correct?

topics.title: Traditional classification and the golden rules

learn.hook: Long before computers, Indian munims kept the bahi-khata with three golden rules. They still give the same answers as the modern equation approach.
points: Traditional classification: personal accounts (persons, firms, companies, banks, capital, drawings); real accounts (assets such as cash, furniture, goodwill); nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains).
Personal account: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.
Capital and drawings are personal accounts of the owner. Outstanding and prepaid expense accounts are representative personal accounts.

example.q: Cash sales ₹15,000. Apply the golden rules.
steps: Accounts: Cash (real) and Sales (nominal, income).
Cash comes in: debit Cash.
Sales is an income: credit Sales.

learn.reallife: An old Marwari firm's munim and a modern ERP system at Infosys will both debit Rent and credit Cash when rent is paid: two methods, one answer.

topics.title: The journal: format, simple and compound entries

learn.hook: The journal is the diary of a business: every transaction enters it first, date by date, before going anywhere else. That's why it's called the book of original entry.
points: Journal: the book of original (prime) entry where transactions are first recorded in chronological order. Recording in it is called journalising.
Format: Date | Particulars (debit account with 'Dr', credit account prefixed with 'To', then narration in brackets) | L.F. (ledger folio) | Debit amount (₹) | Credit amount (₹).
Simple entry: one debit and one credit. Compound entry: more than one debit or more than one credit, e.g. payment with discount.

Typical entries: Capital: Dr Cash / Cr Capital. Cash purchases: Dr Purchases / Cr Cash. Credit sales: Dr Debtor / Cr Sales. Purchases returned: Dr Creditor / Cr Purchases Return. Sales returned: Dr Sales Return / Cr Debtor.
Payment with discount: Dr Creditor (full amount) / Cr Cash (amount paid) / Cr Discount Received (discount).

example.q: Paid ₹19,600 to Sohan in full settlement of ₹20,000 owed to him. Journalise.
steps: Sohan's liability of ₹20,000 is fully cleared: debit Sohan ₹20,000.
Cash paid ₹19,600: credit Cash.
Discount received = 20,000 − 19,600 = ₹400: credit Discount Received (a gain).
example.answer: Dr Sohan ₹20,000 / Cr Cash ₹19,600 / Cr Discount Received ₹400

learn.reallife: Every UPI transfer you make generates a dated record on the bank's server, the digital cousin of a journal entry.

Entry: Dr Cash ₹14,700, Dr Discount Allowed ₹300 / Cr Kiran ₹15,000.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Payment to a creditor with a cash discount is a compound entry.

options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

steps: A: payment to a creditor with discount is a compound entry. True.

Having more than one credit is what makes it compound, so R explains A.

topics.title: Special journal entries: drawings of goods, charity, samples, losses

learn.hook: A sweet shop gives free laddoos to customers as samples, donates boxes to an orphanage on Independence Day, and the owner takes some home for family. Each one is a different entry.
points: Goods taken by the owner for personal use: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods given as charity: Dr Charity / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods distributed as free samples: Dr Advertisement / Cr Purchases (at cost).

Goods lost by fire or theft: Dr Loss by Fire (or Loss by Theft) / Cr Purchases. If insured and a claim is admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (amount admitted), Dr Loss by Fire (balance) / Cr Purchases (cost).
Purchases is credited because these goods were bought for sale but will never be sold; the purchases figure is reduced.

example.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 were destroyed by fire. The insurance company admitted a claim of ₹35,000. Journalise.
steps: Total cost of goods lost = ₹50,000: credit Purchases.
Claim admitted ₹35,000: debit Insurance Claim (an asset, receivable).
Loss not covered = 50,000 − 35,000 = ₹15,000: debit Loss by Fire.
example.answer: Dr Insurance Claim ₹35,000, Dr Loss by Fire ₹15,000 / Cr Purchases ₹50,000

topics.title: Journal entries with GST and set-off of input tax credit

learn.hook: A Delhi gadget dealer pays GST on every purchase and collects GST on every sale. At month-end, she pays the government only the difference. Here is how that shows in the journal.
points: Purchase within the state: Dr Purchases, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Supplier (or Cash). Inter-state purchase: Dr Purchases, Dr Input IGST / Cr Supplier.
Sale within the state: Dr Customer (or Cash) / Cr Sales, Cr Output CGST, Cr Output SGST. Inter-state sale: Cr Output IGST.
GST paid on expenses (e.g. rent, telephone) is also input tax: Dr Expense, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Bank.

Set-off: input IGST is used first against output IGST, then against CGST and SGST. Input CGST is used against output CGST, then IGST. Input SGST is used against output SGST, then IGST. CGST cannot be set off against SGST or vice versa.
Set-off entry: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST (and similarly for SGST). Balance paid: Dr Output CGST, Dr Output SGST / Cr Bank.

example.q: Within Maharashtra, Asha buys goods ₹1,00,000 and sells them for ₹1,50,000; GST 18%. Find CGST payable after set-off and give the set-off entry.
steps: Output CGST = 9% × 1,50,000 = ₹13,500; output SGST = ₹13,500.
Set-off: Dr Output CGST ₹9,000 / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000 (same for SGST).
CGST payable = 13,500 − 9,000 = ₹4,500; SGST payable = ₹4,500.
example.answer: CGST payable ₹4,500 (and SGST ₹4,500); set-off: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000.

Answer: ₹7,000

Answer: Input CGST against output SGST

Dr Input SGST ₹6,000 / Cr Output SGST ₹6,000
quiz.explain: Output tax (a liability) is reduced by debiting it; input tax (an asset) is used up by crediting it.

Input SGST is an asset used up: credit Input SGST ₹6,000.
No bank payment is involved in a set-off.
Answer: Dr Output SGST ₹6,000 / Cr Input SGST ₹6,000

Reason (R): It can be used to reduce future GST liability.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Input tax credit is a right to reduce tax payable, so it is an asset.
steps: A: input CGST is shown on the debit side as an asset. True.
R: it can be used to reduce future GST liability. True.
Being a right to reduce tax payable is why it is an asset, so R explains A.
Both true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks input GST is an expense

quiz.q: Telephone bill ₹5,000 plus 18% GST paid by cheque (intra-state). The total amount credited to Bank is

steps: Answer: ₹5,900
quiz.mistake: Credits only the base amount

quiz.q: Case: In a month, input IGST ₹9,000, output IGST ₹5,000 and output CGST ₹3,000. After using input IGST first against IGST and then against CGST, what IGST credit is left?
quiz.explain: ₹5,000 of input IGST pays output IGST, the next ₹3,000 pays output CGST, leaving ₹1,000.
steps: After IGST: 9,000 − 5,000 = ₹4,000 left
Against CGST: 4,000 − 3,000 = ₹1,000 left
Answer: ₹1,000

topics.title: The ledger: format, utility and classification of accounts

learn.hook: The journal tells you what happened on 12 June. The ledger tells you how much the business owes Gupta Traders today. Different questions, different books.
points: The ledger is the principal book of accounts. It contains all accounts (cash, debtors, sales, rent and so on), each on a separate page or folio.
Format of a ledger account: debit side (left): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount; credit side (right): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount.
Utility: it shows the net position of each account, such as total sales, total expenses, amount owed by each debtor and to each creditor, and its balances are used to prepare the trial balance.

Journal vs ledger: the journal is the book of original entry, records chronologically, and is the basis of posting; the ledger is the principal book, records analytically by accounts, and is the basis of the trial balance.
Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) are balanced and carried forward; temporary accounts (revenues, expenses) are closed by transfer to the trading and profit and loss account.

example.q: Classify as permanent or temporary: Machinery, Wages, Creditors, Commission received, Capital.
steps: Permanent accounts appear in the balance sheet and continue to the next year: Machinery, Creditors, Capital.
Temporary accounts are closed at year-end to the P&L or trading account: Wages, Commission received.
example.answer: Permanent: Machinery, Creditors, Capital; temporary: Wages, Commission received.

topics.title: Posting from the journal and balancing ledger accounts

learn.hook: Posting is like delivering letters: each journal entry has two addresses, the account debited and the account credited, and each must receive its copy.
points: Posting is transferring journal entries to ledger accounts. In the account debited, write the entry on the debit side as 'To [name of the account credited]'. In the account credited, write it on the credit side as 'By [name of the account debited]'.
Compound entries: each debit and each credit is posted separately. In each account, the other side's accounts are named (for one-to-many entries, each counter account is named with its own amount).
Cross references: L.F. in the journal shows the ledger page; J.F. in the ledger shows the journal page. They prove the posting is done and allow tracing.
Balancing: total both sides, put the difference on the smaller side as 'By/To Balance c/d', and bring it down on the opposite side as 'To/By Balance b/d'.

example.q: Entry: Dr Furniture ₹30,000 / Cr Cash ₹30,000. How is it posted?
steps: Furniture A/c (debited): debit side, 'To Cash ₹30,000'.
Cash A/c (credited): credit side, 'By Furniture ₹30,000'.
Write the ledger page in the journal's L.F. column and the journal page in each account's J.F. column.
example.answer: Furniture A/c Dr side: To Cash ₹30,000; Cash A/c Cr side: By Furniture ₹30,000.
